events.title: C++11 standardized
events.summary: ISO/IEC 14882:2011 was published on September 1, 2011 — the C++11 standard with auto, lambdas, move semantics, and smart pointers.
events.about: C++11 was the first major C++ update in 13 years. It added `auto`, range-for loops, lambdas, threads, and smart pointers (`unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`) — so everyday code needed less boilerplate and fewer manual `delete` calls. Most C++ written today uses C++11 or later.

narrative.whyChosen: C++ had barely changed since 1998 while [Java] and C# kept adding modern features. C++11 was the catch-up release that made the language feel current again.
narrative.whyImportant: Developers spent less time fighting the language: `auto` removed repetitive type names, lambdas made callbacks readable, and smart pointers caught memory bugs at compile time instead of in production crashes.
narrative.problemSolved: C++98 code felt verbose and error-prone next to newer languages — especially around memory management and threading. [Teams] wanted modern conveniences without giving up C++'s speed.

events.title: CircleCI founded
events.summary: Paul Biggar and Allen Rohner founded CircleCI on September 1, 2011 — a hosted continuous integration platform for fast, parallel test runs.
events.about: CircleCI connects to GitHub repos and runs builds in Docker containers — parallelizing test suites and caching dependencies for speed. It competed with Travis CI and later GitHub Actions for [SaaS] CI market share. Example: every push to `main` runs lint, unit tests, and deploy previews automatically.

narrative.whyChosen: CircleCI brought container-based, parallel CI to teams that outgrew single-worker Travis builds.
narrative.whyImportant: It helped normalize Docker in CI pipelines before Kubernetes took over production.
narrative.problemSolved: Slow, serial CI blocked developer flow; teams needed faster feedback on every commit.

events.title: WooCommerce released
events.summary: WooThemes released WooCommerce on September 27, 2011 — a WordPress plugin that turned blogs into full online stores.
events.about: WooCommerce adds products, carts, checkout, and payment gateways to any WordPress site — themes and extensions from a huge marketplace. It became the most-used e-commerce stack on the web, later stewarded by Automattic after acquiring WooThemes.

narrative.whyChosen: WooCommerce made WordPress a commerce platform without leaving the CMS ecosystem.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved plugin-based e-commerce could outscale dedicated carts for SMB merchants.
narrative.problemSolved: WordPress site owners needed selling tools without migrating to Magento or hosted [SaaS].

events.title: CSS Selectors Level 3 standard
events.summary: The [W3C] published Selectors Level 3 as a Recommendation on September 29, 2011 — standardizing `:nth-child`, `:not`, attribute selectors, and pseudo-elements.
events.about: Selectors Level 3 was the first major CSS module to reach Recommendation status after CSS 2.1 — adding structural pseudo-classes, [UI] state selectors (`:checked`, `:disabled`), and combinators that jQuery had popularized in JavaScript. Every modern stylesheet uses its patterns for targeting DOM nodes without extra markup.

narrative.whyChosen: Selectors Level 3 was the first CSS3 module to ship as a finished standard.
narrative.whyImportant: It gave authors precise DOM targeting primitives that powered responsive and component-based CSS.
narrative.problemSolved: CSS2 selectors were too limited for dynamic UIs and complex document structures.

events.title: Trello kanban boards launched
events.summary: Fog Creek Software unveiled Trello on September 13, 2011 at TechCrunch Disrupt — a card-based kanban tool that made project tracking feel like drag-and-drop sticky notes.
events.about: Trello's boards, lists, and cards spread from side projects to entire startups — lighter than Jira, more visual than Basecamp. Atlassian acquired it in 2017, but millions of dev teams still run sprint boards and bug triage columns on Trello before graduating to heavier tools.

narrative.whyChosen: Trello popularized kanban PM for developers who hated enterprise issue trackers.
narrative.whyImportant: Its card [UI] became the template for lightweight agile boards everywhere.
narrative.problemSolved: Jira was overkill for small teams that just needed visible work-in-progress.
